title: feel the same way (about + noun / as + person)
front_html: feel the same way (about + noun / as + person)
back_html:
Say that you share another person’s opinion or emotional reaction. About introduces the topic; as introduces the person or comparison clause. A comparison clause can also follow directly: the same way he did. This expresses a shared feeling, not merely understanding why someone feels it.

Examples:

• I feel the same way about having fewer meetings; uninterrupted time helps me concentrate.
• She felt the same way as I did after the interview. / I’d probably feel the same way he did in that situation.

title: That way, + clause
front_html: That way, + clause
back_html:
Refer back to an action or suggestion and explain how it makes a result possible. That way often introduces a consequence with can, will, could, or would; it does not require a hypothetical condition.

Examples:

• Let’s record the decisions. That way, everyone can check what we agreed on.
• I’ll take an earlier train. That way, I’ll have time to find the meeting room.
• I’d practice with a partner. That way, I could get immediate feedback.

title: I wouldn't be surprised if + clause
front_html: I wouldn't be surprised if + clause
back_html:
Say that an outcome seems plausible or expected. A past-form verb after if can describe a future possibility, not just past time. Wouldn’t here softens the expectation; it does not mean the outcome is impossible.

Examples:

• I wouldn’t be surprised if the deadline slipped; we still have several unresolved issues.
• I wouldn’t be surprised if she accepted the offer; the role suits her experience.

modest / humble

back_html:
modest / humble
modest: adjective · humble: adjective · verb
modest: /ˈmɑdəst/
humble: /ˈhʌmbəl/ [Anki audio]
ACTIVE

modest

ADJECTIVE
1. Not boasting about your achievements or abilities.
She remained modest about her achievements.
2. Not very large, expensive, or ambitious.
We made a modest improvement in response time.

humble

ADJECTIVE
1. Not treating yourself as more important than other people.
He stayed humble despite his success.
2. Simple or low in social status.
She came from humble beginnings.
VERB
1. Make someone feel less proud or more aware of their limits.
The defeat humbled the team.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
Someone has achieved something without boasting.“She is modest about her success.” / “She remains humble despite her success.”Both are natural. Modest often highlights how someone presents achievements; humble can emphasize their attitude toward themselves.
You describe a small amount or limited change.“We made a modest improvement.”Modest is the ordinary choice for a limited amount; humble does not usually describe the size of an improvement.
You describe simple circumstances.“They lived in a modest home.” / “They lived in a humble home.”Both can describe simplicity. Humble can draw more attention to low status or lack of luxury.

Difference / overlap

Modest and humble overlap when describing someone who does not boast. Neither word automatically means lacking confidence. Keep their other senses distinct: a modest increase; humble beginnings; an experience that humbled someone.

Common patterns

modest: be modest about + achievements; a modest budget/improvement
humble: remain/stay humble; humble beginnings; a humble home; be humbled by + experience
Synonyms
modest
1. humble — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; overlaps in not boasting.
1. limited — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for size or extent.
humble
1. modest — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; overlaps in not boasting.
1. modest — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for simple circumstances.
Antonyms
modest
1. boastful — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.
1. substantial — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; for an amount or improvement.
humble
1. arrogant — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

Patterns on this card:

scrape / scrap
scrape: verb · noun · scrap: noun · verb
scrape: /skreɪp/
scrap: /skræp/ [Anki audio]
ACTIVE

scrape

VERB
1. Rub a surface against something rough, or remove material by rubbing it with a hard edge.
Scrape the old paint off before repainting the door.
2. Damage skin or another surface by rubbing it against something rough or sharp.
I scraped my knee on the pavement.
NOUN
1. A shallow injury or mark caused by rubbing against something rough.
She had a small scrape on her elbow.

scrap

NOUN
1. A small leftover piece of something.
Save that scrap of paper.
2. Discarded material that can be reused or recycled.
The old pipes were sold as scrap.
VERB
1. Abandon a plan or discard something that is no longer wanted.
We scrapped the proposal because it was too expensive.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
A rough surface damages your skin.“I scraped my knee.”Use scrape for the rubbing action or shallow injury. Scrap does not describe this injury.
You remove material from a surface.“Scrape the paint off the door.”Scrape describes how the material is removed.
You decide not to continue a plan.“We scrapped the plan.”Scrap means abandon or discard; it does not involve rubbing.
You describe a leftover piece.“Write it on a scrap of paper.” / “There is a scrape on my elbow.”Scrap names a leftover piece; scrape can name a shallow injury.

Difference / overlap

Scrape /skreɪp/ and scrap /skræp/ have different vowels and meanings. Scrape commonly concerns rubbing, removing, or shallow damage. Scrap commonly concerns leftover/discarded material or abandoning a plan. Scrape by remains a separate phrasal verb.

Common patterns

scrape: scrape your knee; scrape paint off a surface; scrape something against a wall. Scrape by is a separate phrasal verb meaning manage with barely enough.
scrap: a scrap of paper/fabric; scrap metal; food scraps; scrap a plan/proposal
Synonyms

1. scrub — RELATED; usually repeated rubbing to clean, not necessarily with a hard edge.

1. abandon — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for a plan.

compromise

NOUN
1. an agreement reached by accepting less than originally wanted.
We reached a compromise on the deadline.
VERB
1. accept less than originally wanted to reach agreement.
We compromised on the deadline.
2. weaken or put something at risk.

meet halfway

IDIOM
1. Accept part of another person's wishes so both sides can agree.
If you can extend the deadline, I'll meet you halfway on the scope.

concede

VERB
1. Admit that something is true, or yield something after resisting.
I concede that your approach is simpler.

give in

PHRASAL VERB
1. Stop resisting and agree to a demand or temptation.
I finally gave in and agreed to help.

back down

PHRASAL VERB
1. Withdraw a position or demand after opposition.
She refused to back down on the deadline.

Everyday situations: what you can say

SituationNatural sentencesWhat to notice
Two sides adjust their demands.“We compromised on the deadline.” / “We met each other halfway on the deadline.”Both work for mutual adjustment.
Someone yields in a negotiation.“They conceded on the deadline.”Concede can mean yield something after resisting.
You acknowledge a point.“I concede that your approach is simpler.”Concede that + clause means admit a point; it need not mean accept a demand.
Someone stops resisting.“She finally gave in.” / “She finally backed down.”Often overlapping; neither requires a mutual compromise.
An action puts something at risk.“Sharing passwords compromises security.”Compromise also means weaken or endanger.

Difference / overlap

Compromise and meet someone halfway often describe the same mutual adjustment. Concede can mean admit a point or yield something. Give in and back down often overlap for stopping resistance; neither requires both sides to adjust. Compromise security means put security at risk, not negotiate.

Common patterns

compromise: reach a compromise; compromise with someone on something; compromise security
meet halfway: meet someone halfway; meet each other halfway
concede: concede that + clause; concede a point; concede defeat; make a concession (the related noun phrase). We made a concession on the deadline to reach an agreement. A concession is something you agree to give up or allow; it need not mean that both sides compromise.
give in: give in to + pressure/demand/temptation
back down: back down on/from + position/demand; refuse to back down
Synonyms
compromise
1. agreement — RELATED; for the noun.
2. meet halfway — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for mutual adjustment.
meet halfway
1. compromise — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; in negotiation.
concede
1. admit — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for acknowledging a fact.
2. yield — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; for giving way.
give in
1. yield — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; more formal.
back down
1. give in — NEAR-INTERCHANGEABLE; in many disputes.
Antonyms
compromise
No useful antonym for this word.
meet halfway
No useful antonym for this word.
concede
1. deny — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; of admitting a claim.
give in
1. hold out — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE; when continuing to resist.
back down
1. stand firm — CONTEXTUAL OPPOSITE.

title: In my experience, + clause · As far as I know, + clause · From what I have heard, + clause · Apparently, + clause
front_html: In my experience, + clause · As far as I know, + clause · From what I have heard, + clause · Apparently, + clause
back_html:
Patterns on this card:
In my experience, + clause · As far as I know, + clause · From what I have heard, + clause · Apparently, + clause

Identify the basis or limits of a claim. Experience means firsthand experience; as far as I know allows for missing information. The related expression as far as I can tell limits a judgment to available observations; it overlaps with as far as I know when those observations are the basis of your knowledge. From what I have heard identifies a report. Apparently presents something as seeming true from reports or evidence, without guaranteeing it.

Examples:

• In my experience, written decisions reduce misunderstandings across time zones.
• As far as I know, the office is still open on Fridays.
• As far as I can tell, the rollout succeeded; the error rate is back to normal.
• From what I have heard, the new manager is very approachable.
• Apparently, the venue has changed; I just received a new invitation.

title: I am sure/certain/convinced/confident (that) + clause
front_html: I am sure/certain/convinced/confident (that) + clause
back_html:
State a strong belief or assurance. Sure and certain are close alternatives; convinced stresses that you hold a belief firmly. Confident often stresses assurance about an outcome or ability. Context allows substantial overlap; the wording does not prove the claim. Pretty sure softens sure: you feel fairly confident while leaving room for doubt.

Examples:

• I am sure this is the right address. / I am certain this is the right address. / I am pretty sure this is the right address.
• I am convinced that the old process needs to change.
• I am confident that we can finish the migration this month.

title: simple past · had + past participle · had been + V-ing
front_html: simple past · had + past participle · had been + V-ing
back_html:
Patterns on this card:
simple past · had + past participle · had been + V-ing

Use the simple past for the main events in a past account. Use the past perfect when you need to look back from one past moment to an earlier event. Do not use the past perfect merely because an event happened a long time ago.

Use had been + V-ing to look back at an activity continuing up to a past moment. Had just/barely + past participle + when places an action shortly before another event; barely emphasizes how little time passed. In I’d just sat down, I’d means I had; in I’d ask, it means I would.

Examples:

• I had just sent the proposal when the client called. / I sent the proposal and then called the client.
• I’d barely fallen asleep when the alarm went off.
• She ate before the meeting. / She was not hungry because she had eaten before the meeting.
• After I finished the report, I sent it. / By the time I sent the report, I had checked every figure.
• I had been waiting for an hour when the clinic finally called my name.

title: C04-043
front_html:
Match each completed frame to its conventional emphasis.


1. experience of recovering from surgery
2. experience with statistical software
3. experience in statistical analysis/working with children
back_html:
1. experience of + event/process can foreground a lived experience.
2. experience with + tool/system often foregrounds hands-on familiarity.
3. experience in + domain/activity often foregrounds skill or work in that
area.


Of, with, and in overlap in practical-experience contexts; these
are useful tendencies rather than absolute categories.


To emphasize acquiring practical skills, use gain experience in + domain/activity.


- I want to gain experience in system design.
